newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan holds security summit amid crime concerns.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan holds security summit amid crime concerns.

text.p: Taiwan President Lee Teng-hui convened a security summit on Friday to try to assuage public fears over a worsening crime problem following the kidnap and murder of a popular actress's daughter.
Lee called the meeting amid news that more than 20,000 people planned to march in Taipei on Sunday to protest what they see as the government's inability to stamp out crime.

"The president was concerned about the wave of crimes that emerged recently and thus called the meeting to address the law and order issue," a spokesman from Lee's presidential office said by telephone.
He said the president had decided to cancel some of his planned activities to host the meeting, which would be attended by top government officials and military leaders.
Taiwan's people were shocked and grief-stricken after police on Monday found the body of 17-year-old Pai Hsiao-yen, daughter of actress Pai Ping-ping, floating naked in a river.
Police said the kidnappers, who remained at large, had strangled the teenager with two ropes, bound her hands and sunk her in the river with weights.
The murder prompted lawmakers and people to call for the resignation of Vice President Lien Chan, who doubles as premier, and other officials for failing to maintain social stability.
Lee had said in a statement that he was "extremely saddened" and "outraged by the criminals' inhuman method".
Pai's gruesome murder followed a string of violent crimes that have haunted Taiwan since November 1996.
In November 1996, two gunmen broke into the home of northern Taoyuan county magistrate Liu Pang-yu and killed eight people, including Liu, in a gangland-style execution.
One week later, women's rights activist Peng Wan-ju was raped and stabbed to death in southern Kaohsiung. Police found 35 knife wounds in her naked body.
Interior Minister Lin Feng-cheng acknowledged in December that Taiwan's social order had deteriorated to a "shocking" level, with crime rate soaring by 80 percent from 1990 to 1996.
Anti-crime activists said the murder of Pai Hsiao-yen was the latest example of how the government was failing to protect its people.

"Pai's case was the last straw. And we could no longer tolerate the government's inability to stamp out crime," said Feng Hsien-hsien, executive director of the Peng Wan-ju Foundation, set up after the murder of the feminist.
"This was why we decided to join forces to stage a large-scale march on Sunday to demand that the government improve law and order in Taiwan," she told Reuters.

Lee Tien-chien, executive secretary of the Humanistic Educational Foundation, a major organiser of the march, said some 20,000 people from 100 civilian groups have registered to join the Taipei march.
"We will ask the president to acknowledge (his) mistake and to reshuffle the cabinet," he said.
Government statistics show that 149 kidnap cases were registered in Taiwan in 1996.
